strengths: Addresses an important and timely meta-evaluation question: whether proliferating LLM benchmarks measure distinct capabilities or overlapping ones.
Proposes an interesting idea of using in-the-wild perplexity patterns as benchmark signatures, and compares this view against semantic similarity and performance correlations.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering 32 models and 88 benchmark/sub-benchmark tasks across MMLU, BBH, MBPP, and IFEval.
The paper usefully highlights that raw performance correlations can be dominated by benchmark family and question format, which is a real concern for benchmark-agreement studies.
weaknesses: The central signature methodology is not sufficiently validated. Signatures are selected from token-level perplexities to predict the same benchmark performance vectors that are later used to infer benchmark overlap, creating a strong risk of circularity and overfitting.

The statistical setting is extremely underdetermined: roughly 32 model observations are used to screen millions of token features and select around 30 features per benchmark. AIC forward selection is not convincing in this regime, and the reported leave-one-out result is not enough unless all screening and selection are nested inside each fold and tested on truly unseen models.

The interpretation of low perplexity as training exposure or capability familiarity is too strong. Perplexity is confounded by model scale, architecture, tokenizer, instruction tuning, corpus overlap, and general language modeling quality.

Token-level comparisons across heterogeneous models and tokenizers are underspecified. It is unclear whether last-token perplexities are comparable across models with different tokenization and context handling.

The semantic-overlap baseline appears weak: concatenating and truncating benchmark questions can discard most items and may make the comparison highly order-dependent, so it is not a strong baseline for semantic redundancy.

The paper makes broad claims about benchmark validity, capability space, and benchmark design, but provides mostly correlational heatmaps and limited statistical controls. There is little ground-truth validation that signature overlap corresponds to actual shared capabilities.
Reproducibility is limited: the exact selected signatures, code, random seeds, preprocessing details, and full numerical overlap matrices are not provided in the manuscript.

Presentation has several clarity and polish issues, including inconsistent algorithm descriptions, typographical errors, and imprecise claims such as signatures 'filtering out noise' without adequate justification.

strengths: The paper tackles an important meta-evaluation problem: understanding overlap and redundancy among LLM benchmarks beyond raw score correlations.
The proposed notion of benchmark signatures from in-the-wild perplexity patterns is creative and potentially useful as a complementary diagnostic.
The empirical setup is reasonably ambitious, using 32 models, 88 benchmark tasks/subtasks, and a large RedPajama-derived corpus, with comparisons to semantic and performance-level overlap.
The paper clearly illustrates a real concern: performance correlations can be dominated by benchmark family or question format rather than intended capability.
weaknesses: The main methodology is statistically fragile. It selects from millions of token features with only 32 model observations, then applies stepwise AIC; this creates severe multiple-comparison and overfitting risk. The LOOCV evidence is not enough unless the entire feature-selection pipeline is nested and independently validated.

The evaluation is partly circular: signatures are chosen because they predict benchmark performance across the same model set, and overlap is then computed using the same models' perplexities. This makes it hard to know whether the signatures capture capabilities, model-family effects, size, calibration, or artifacts of the selection procedure.

The central interpretation that low perplexity reflects training exposure, familiarity, or capacity is asserted much more strongly than supported. Perplexity is confounded by tokenizer differences, architecture, model scale, instruction tuning, calibration, and unknown training data.

Baselines and ablations are insufficient. The paper needs comparisons to random or matched token signatures, Lasso/ridge/CCA/PCA-style alternatives, corpus/sample-size sensitivity, model-subset stability, preselection-threshold sensitivity, and validation on held-out models or benchmarks.

The semantic-overlap baseline is weak: concatenating questions and truncating to an embedding model's maximum length likely discards much of the benchmark content and may explain the narrow similarity range.

The claimed breadth of 88 benchmarks is somewhat overstated because many are MMLU and BBH subfields/tasks rather than independent benchmark suites. This limits the strength of conclusions about benchmark design broadly.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact RedPajama version/sampling, tokenization across heterogeneous models, prompts/evaluation settings, seeds, selected signature examples, raw overlap matrices, and code/data release are not sufficiently specified.
Several conclusions, such as signatures being robust to format/family bias or revealing an interconnected capacity space, are plausible but too strong relative to the evidence provided.

The signature-overlap analysis is partly circular: signatures are selected because they predict benchmark performance across the same model population, then overlap is inferred from correlations of those selected features across models. The claim that signatures resolve benchmark-family or question-format bias is overstrong. The comparison is mainly against naive performance correlations, without stronger controls such as partialing out model strength, size, family, instruction tuning, tokenizer effects, or using factor/IRT-style benchmark agreement baselines.

The semantic baseline is weak and likely underestimates semantic overlap. Concatenating benchmark questions and truncating to an embedding model context window discards most items and makes the narrow similarity range unsurprising. There is no ground-truth or synthetic validation showing that the method recovers known benchmark overlaps or known independent capabilities. As a result, the interpretation of heatmaps as a map of LLM capacity space remains speculative.

Several major empirical conclusions rely on imbalanced or singleton categories, such as coding, instruction following, and AbsenceBench, making cross-function claims fragile. Some example signatures appear semantically unrelated to the claimed benchmark functions, suggesting possible spurious correlations.

The paper makes strong causal or mechanistic language about training exposure, acquired capacity, and benchmark validity, but perplexity on RedPajama-like corpora only provides a correlational proxy and may mostly reflect model family, scale, corpus overlap, or tokenization differences.

Reproducibility and presentation have issues: the abstract ends with an incomplete open-source sentence, code/data URL is missing, notation and formulas contain errors, some dimensionalities are inconsistent, and there are multiple typos such as the evaluation harness name. These issues reduce confidence in the implementation details.
